claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering or localized elemental segregation governs whether initially single-phase high-entropy nanoparticles remain structurally and chemically stable from 473 to 1923 K.
Specific interatomic interactions among the constituent metals give rise to short-range ordering or localized segregation.
Nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal ratios can initially form a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
The Co/Mo atomic ratio can be controllably varied in single-solid-solution CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles.
Changing the Co/Mo ratio modulates the propensity of these nanoparticles to develop short-range chemical ordering.
The catalytic activity of CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles can be tuned by changing the Co/Mo ratio.
Controlled atmospheres avoid oxidation during high-temperature testing.
Differential bonding interactions among the constituent metals lead to local chemical ordering.
Interactions that favor a uniform elemental distribution stabilize the single-phase solid solution.
Interactions that favor segregation cause local phase separation.
Surface microstructural changes alter catalytic active sites and thereby affect catalytic performance.
Surface microstructural changes associated with ordering or segregation affect thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles that maintain a uniform elemental distribution will retain structural integrity and stable catalytic behavior.
Nanoparticles that maintain a uniform elemental distribution will exhibit stable thermoelectric behavior.
Pronounced local ordering or segregation will degrade structural, catalytic, and thermoelectric properties relative to the initial single-phase state.
The proposed governing relationship applies throughout 473–1923 K to near-equiatomic nanoparticles under controlled atmospheres.
Changing composition, environment, or particle size may introduce alternative stabilizing or destabilizing mechanisms.
A lack of correlation between ordering or segregation and catalytic and thermoelectric performance would falsify the proposed governing relationship.
